awd_titl_txt: Conference: Remote Sensing and Fluxes for Real-world Impact: Integration with Advanced Techniques
awd_abstract_narration:
This workshop is designed to help the next generation of scientists who study carbon, water, and energy in managed ecosystems. Data collected from tall towers positioned above vegetation allow scientists to measure how water, carbon dioxide, and energy move between ecosystems and the atmosphere. Expanding these local measurements to cover larger areas—such as regions or continents—helps improve our understanding of how ecosystems work and how they respond to changes in climate and land use. Building on recent advances in the field, this workshop will give early-career researchers the chance to learn about the latest tools, work with real-world data, and get advice from experienced scientists in different fields. Hands-on activities will let participants practice using online tools and new data and learn how to apply these tools in realistic situations. They will also learn how to work with people from other fields, like business and government. The workshop will focus on building strong, clear ways to measure and report the amount of carbon and water that moves between ecosystem and the atmosphere. This helps make climate projects more trustworthy and useful. 

This workshop tackles major scientific challenges in expanding local data to broader scales. It brings together experienced researchers, early-career scientists, and industry professionals to improve methods for combining ground-based measurements with detailed satellite imagery. Sessions will focus on aligning the scale of different data sources, estimating how far each tower’s data can be applied, and checking results across multiple study locations. By creating clear, adaptable methods for tracking carbon, water, and energy across different landscapes, the workshop will support better environmental monitoring. The improved data can be used to strengthen ecosystem models, provide more accurate information about how natural systems cycle nutrients and energy, and support smarter decisions about managing land and natural resources. Through hands-on training and group work, participants will gain practical tools to apply these methods to real-world environmental challenges and help shape future research.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
In March 2026, 55 researchers, practitioners, early-career scientists, and industry partners gathered in Boulder, Colorado, for a two-day workshop supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF Award 2532339). The workshop, Remote Sensing and Fluxes for Real-World Impact: Integration with Advanced Techniques, was organized through a collaboration of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON/Battelle), AmeriFlux (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory), and the CarbonDew Community of Practice, building directly on a prior workshop held in Berkeley, California in July 2024. An additional 18 participants attended virtually, bringing total engagement to 73 participants.

The central challenge the workshop addressed is how to take precise measurements made at a single field site, such as the carbon, water, and energy exchanges captured by a flux tower, and reliably translate them into information useful at landscape, regional, or continental scales. This question is increasingly urgent as society demands credible environmental data for carbon measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV), water management, and sustainability reporting.

Over two days, participants moved from foundational concepts through hands-on tutorials to collaborative group projects. Tutorial activities provided participants with practical experience integrating flux tower data and remote sensing products using scalable workflows and explored emerging methods for flux spatialization, cross-site validation, Earth observation foundation models, and AI-based geo-embedding.

Four overarching outcomes emerged. First, participants agreed that flux measurements must remain the foundation for scaling and AI applications. Second, the workshop established a four-level scaling hierarchy that advances the nested scaling paradigm identified as a priority during the 2024 workshop. Third, the workshop clarified the importance of dynamic flux footprints, representative flux source areas, and cross-site validation. Fourth, participants emphasized the need for shared operational infrastructure, including quality-control pipelines, benchmark datasets, cloud-based workflows, and decision-support dashboards.

Application areas demonstrated at the workshop included evapotranspiration products for irrigation, carbon MRV for nature-based climate solutions, supply-chain carbon disclosure, and ecosystem forecasting. A career roundtable expanded participant engagement and career path mentorship.

Participants organized into five collaborative project groups addressing flux patterns across land-cover types, links between ecological and flux variation, comparisons of flux maps with coarser satellite products, shared research infrastructure for proposals, and the scientific interpretation of AI-generated geo-embeddings.

Following the workshop, organizers furnished materials through a public repository (remote-sensing-flux-upscaling-workshop-2026), workshop summary report, a blog post (NEON Live: Connecting Flux Data, Remote Sensing and AI), and the Remote Sensing and Flux Upscaling Community. Four working groups continue to work toward manuscripts, open-source tools, datasets, and a journal special issue.

The workshop reinforced that progress at the intersection of flux science, remote sensing, and AI depends on sustained collaboration across academic, governmental, and private-sector communities. The resulting working groups, repositories, and planned publications provide a durable foundation for continued progress.
